questions.question: What type of IP address is automatically assigned to every EC2 instance when launched inside a VPC?

options.text: Public IP
Elastic IP
Private IP
IPv6 address

explanation.correct: Every EC2 instance automatically receives a private IP address from its subnet's CIDR range upon launch.
explanation.why: Public IPs must be explicitly requested. Elastic IPs must be allocated and associated manually. IPv6 is optional.

questions.question: Which RFC defines the three reserved private IP address ranges?

options.text: RFC 2616
RFC 1918
RFC 4271
RFC 793

explanation.correct: RFC 1918 (Address Allocation for Private Internets, February 1996) defines the three private IP ranges.
explanation.why: RFC 2616 is HTTP/1.1, RFC 4271 is BGP, RFC 793 is TCP.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three RFC 1918 private IP ranges?

explanation.correct: 169.254.0.0/16 is the link-local range (APIPA), not an RFC 1918 private range.
explanation.why: The three RFC 1918 ranges are 10.0.0.0/8 (24-bit block), 172.16.0.0/12 (20-bit block), and 192.168.0.0/16 (16-bit block).

questions.question: How many IP addresses does AWS reserve in each subnet?

explanation.correct: AWS reserves 5 IP addresses in every subnet — the first 4 and the last 1.
explanation.why: This means a /24 subnet (256 addresses) has only 251 usable IPs, not 256.

questions.question: What happens to an EC2 instance's public IP address when it is stopped and restarted?

options.text: It stays the same
It changes to a new public IP
It is converted to an Elastic IP
It is removed permanently

explanation.correct: Standard public IPs in AWS are ephemeral — they change every time the instance is stopped and started.
explanation.why: This is the key limitation of regular public IPs and the reason Elastic IPs exist.

questions.question: Which IP type in AWS is static and does not change when an instance is stopped?

options.text: Private IP
Public IP
Elastic IP
Dynamic IP

explanation.correct: Elastic IP is a static public IPv4 address that remains fixed until you explicitly release it.
explanation.why: Private IPs also persist but are not routable over the internet. Regular public IPs are ephemeral.

questions.question: In AWS, who acts as the Internet Service Provider (ISP)?

options.text: Your local ISP
The Internet Gateway
AWS itself
Route 53

explanation.correct: AWS acts as the ISP for resources inside the cloud. AWS assigns both private IPs (within VPC) and public IPs.
explanation.why: You are not using Jio, Airtel, or any external ISP. AWS owns and manages the IP address pools.

questions.question: What is a Bastion Host?

options.text: A managed database service
A public-facing EC2 instance used as a secure gateway to private subnet resources
A load balancer for private EC2 instances
A DNS resolver for VPCs

explanation.correct: A Bastion Host (or Jump Server) is an EC2 instance in a public subnet that provides secure SSH/RDP access to EC2 instances in private subnets.
explanation.why: It acts as a single controlled entry point — you SSH into the Bastion, then from the Bastion into private instances.

questions.question: In which subnet must a Bastion Host be placed?

options.text: Private subnet
Isolated subnet
Public subnet
Any subnet

explanation.correct: A Bastion Host must be in a public subnet so it can be reached from the internet.
explanation.why: It needs a public IP (or Elastic IP) to be reachable. Private subnets have no direct internet access.

questions.question: What is the default maximum number of Elastic IPs per AWS region per account?

explanation.correct: AWS allows a maximum of 5 Elastic IPs per region per account by default. You can request a limit increase.
explanation.why: This limit exists to conserve the globally limited IPv4 address space.

questions.question: When is an Elastic IP charged by AWS?

options.text: Always, hourly
Only when associated with a stopped instance
Only when allocated but NOT associated with a running instance
Never — it is always free

explanation.correct: AWS charges for Elastic IPs that are allocated but not in use (not associated with a running instance) to discourage IPv4 address waste.
explanation.why: An EIP attached to a running instance is free. An idle EIP wastes a global IPv4 address.

questions.question: Two EC2 instances in the same VPC want to communicate. Which IP type should they use?

options.text: Public IP
Elastic IP
Private IP
NAT IP

explanation.correct: EC2 instances in the same VPC communicate using private IPs. This keeps traffic on the internal AWS network without incurring internet data transfer costs.
explanation.why: Using public IPs for internal VPC traffic would be wasteful, slower, and costs more.

questions.question: A company wants to ensure their web server's public IP never changes after restarts. What should they use?

options.text: Assign a static public IP at launch
Use an Elastic IP
Use a NAT Gateway
Enable enhanced networking

explanation.correct: Elastic IP is the correct choice — it is a fixed public IPv4 address that persists across stop/start cycles and can be associated with any EC2 instance in the account.
explanation.why: Standard public IPs change on restart. NAT Gateway is for outbound traffic from private subnets. Enhanced networking is a performance feature.

questions.question: A developer needs to SSH into a private EC2 instance with no public IP. The company policy prohibits opening port 22 from the internet. What is the BEST solution?

options.text: Assign a public IP to the private EC2
Use a Bastion Host
Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager
Move the EC2 to a public subnet

explanation.correct: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager allows access to private EC2 instances without opening port 22, without a Bastion Host, and without any public IP.
explanation.why: It uses the SSM Agent which connects outbound over HTTPS (port 443) to the SSM endpoint. No inbound ports required.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about NAT Gateway?

options.text: It allows inbound internet connections to private EC2 instances
It must be placed in a private subnet
It allows private EC2 instances to initiate outbound internet connections
It is free to use

explanation.correct: NAT Gateway allows private EC2 instances to initiate outbound connections (e.g., for package updates) without being reachable from the internet.
explanation.why: NAT = Network Address Translation. It translates the private IP to the NAT Gateway's public EIP for outbound traffic only.

questions.question: In which subnet should a NAT Gateway be deployed?

options.text: Private subnet
Public subnet
Any subnet
Isolated subnet

explanation.correct: A NAT Gateway must be placed in a public subnet because it needs to communicate with the Internet Gateway.
explanation.why: The private subnet's route table then points 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to the NAT Gateway.

questions.question: What does a private subnet's route table need to allow EC2 instances to use a NAT Gateway?

options.text: A route 0.0.0.0/0 → Internet Gateway
A route 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT Gateway
A route 0.0.0.0/0 → Bastion Host
No changes needed

explanation.correct: The private subnet's route table must have a rule: destination 0.0.0.0/0, target: NAT Gateway ID.
explanation.why: Without this route, the private EC2 has no path to the NAT Gateway and cannot reach the internet.

questions.question: What is the key difference between NAT Gateway and NAT Instance?

options.text: NAT Gateway is a free service; NAT Instance costs money
NAT Gateway is fully managed by AWS; NAT Instance is an EC2 you manage yourself
NAT Instance supports higher bandwidth than NAT Gateway
NAT Gateway requires Security Groups; NAT Instance does not

explanation.correct: NAT Gateway is a fully managed AWS service that scales automatically. NAT Instance is just an EC2 configured to do NAT — you manage patching, availability, and scaling yourself.
explanation.why: NAT Gateway also scales to 100 Gbps automatically. NAT Instance is limited by instance type and is a single point of failure.

questions.question: Which IP address persists (stays the same) when an EC2 instance is stopped and started?

options.text: Public IP only
Private IP only
Both private IP and Elastic IP
All IP types persist

explanation.correct: The private IP persists across stop/start. If an Elastic IP is associated, it also persists. The standard public IP changes.
explanation.why: This is a common exam trap — make sure you know which IPs are stable and which are ephemeral.

questions.question: A company's Bastion Host was terminated by mistake. They now cannot access their private EC2 instances. They had an Elastic IP attached to the Bastion. What should they do?

options.text: Launch a new Bastion in the private subnet
Launch a new Bastion in the public subnet and associate the same Elastic IP to it
The Elastic IP is lost when the instance is terminated
Contact AWS Support to restore the terminated instance

explanation.correct: Elastic IPs remain in your account after an instance is terminated — they become unassociated. You can associate the same EIP with the new Bastion, preserving all existing whitelisting rules.
explanation.why: This is a key advantage of Elastic IP — it enables quick failover and recovery scenarios.

questions.question: A security audit finds that your Bastion Host Security Group allows SSH from 0.0.0.0/0. What is the risk and how should you fix it?

options.text: No risk — SSH is encrypted so anyone connecting is safe
Risk: Anyone on the internet can attempt to brute-force the Bastion. Fix: Restrict SSH to specific trusted IPs only
Risk: The Bastion will use too much bandwidth. Fix: Use a NAT Instance instead
No fix needed — AWS WAF blocks brute force automatically

explanation.correct: Allowing SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 means anyone on the internet can attempt to connect. Attackers continuously scan for open port 22. You should restrict inbound SSH to your office/home IP or a specific CIDR range.
explanation.why: This is the most common security misconfiguration with Bastion Hosts.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key advantage of AWS Session Manager over a Bastion Host? (Select TWO)

options.text: Session Manager is cheaper than a Bastion Host
Session Manager requires no open inbound ports
Session Manager does not require SSH keys
Session Manager only works with Windows instances

explanation.correct: Session Manager requires no open inbound ports (uses outbound HTTPS from SSM Agent) and requires no SSH keys (uses IAM permissions instead).
explanation.why: These two features make Session Manager significantly more secure than a traditional Bastion Host.

questions.question: You are designing a highly available architecture. Your NAT Gateway is in us-east-1a. An EC2 in us-east-1b needs to route through it. What is the availability risk?

options.text: No risk — NAT Gateway is highly available across all AZs
If AZ us-east-1a goes down, the EC2 in us-east-1b loses outbound internet access
NAT Gateway automatically moves to us-east-1b during a failure
The EC2 will automatically use the Internet Gateway instead

explanation.correct: NAT Gateway is highly available within its AZ but not cross-AZ. If the AZ hosting the NAT Gateway fails, EC2 instances in other AZs that route to it will lose outbound internet access.
explanation.why: Best practice: Deploy one NAT Gateway per AZ and configure each AZ's private subnet route table to use the NAT Gateway in that AZ.

questions.question: An Elastic IP was previously attached to Instance A (now terminated). You want to attach it to Instance B in a different subnet. What is possible?

options.text: Not possible — EIP is tied to the original subnet
Not possible — EIP is tied to the original instance
Possible — EIP can be associated with any instance in the same region
Possible only if both instances are in the same AZ

explanation.correct: An Elastic IP belongs to your AWS account in a region. It can be associated with any EC2 instance in any subnet or AZ within that region.
explanation.why: This is what makes EIPs powerful for failover — you can point the same IP to a replacement instance instantly.

questions.question: A private EC2 runs sudo yum update but times out. The VPC has an Internet Gateway attached. The private subnet's route table only has the local route (10.0.0.0/16 → local). What is missing?

options.text: A Security Group rule allowing port 80 outbound
A NAT Gateway in the public subnet and a route 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT Gateway in the private subnet's route table
A public IP on the private EC2
VPC Flow Logs enabled

explanation.correct: The private subnet has no route to the internet. A NAT Gateway must be created in a public subnet, and the private subnet's route table needs 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT Gateway ID.
explanation.why: The Internet Gateway alone doesn't help private subnets. Private subnets need NAT Gateway to initiate outbound connections.

questions.question: Which statement about RFC 1918 addresses is correct?

options.text: RFC 1918 addresses can be assigned as public internet addresses if needed
RFC 1918 defines addresses reserved permanently for private networks, never routable on the public internet
RFC 1918 only applies to AWS networks
RFC 1918 covers IPv6 addresses

explanation.correct: RFC 1918 addresses (10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, 192.168.x.x) are permanently reserved for private use. Internet routers are configured to drop these addresses if they appear on the public internet.
explanation.why: This is a global standard applied to all networks worldwide, not just AWS.

questions.question: A company has an EC2 with Elastic IP 54.200.10.5. The instance fails. They launch a replacement instance. What must they do to maintain the same IP for customers?

options.text: Nothing — the new instance will automatically get the same EIP
Disassociate the EIP from the failed instance, then associate it with the new instance
Release the EIP and request a new one with the same address
Contact AWS Support to transfer the EIP

explanation.correct: EIPs must be manually disassociated from the failed/old instance and then associated with the new instance. This can be done via console or API and takes seconds.
explanation.why: This manual re-association is often automated in production using Lambda or AWS Systems Manager runbooks.

questions.question: You need to allow a private EC2 to download software packages from the internet, but absolutely no inbound connections from the internet are permitted. Which architecture is correct?

options.text: Assign a public IP to the EC2 and add a Security Group rule denying all inbound
Place the EC2 in a public subnet with NAT rules
Place the EC2 in a private subnet with a route to a NAT Gateway in a public subnet
Use VPC peering to connect to a public VPC

explanation.correct: A private subnet + NAT Gateway is the correct pattern. NAT allows outbound-initiated traffic only. No inbound connections are possible to the private EC2 from the internet.
explanation.why: NAT Gateway is stateful — it allows outbound connections and their return traffic, but blocks any connection initiated from the outside.

questions.question: What happens to an Elastic IP if the EC2 instance it is associated with is TERMINATED (not stopped)?

options.text: The EIP is automatically released back to AWS
The EIP stays in your account as an unassociated EIP and starts accruing charges
The EIP is transferred to another instance automatically
The EIP is converted to a standard public IP

explanation.correct: When an instance is terminated, the associated EIP becomes unattached but remains in your account. Since it is now allocated but not associated with a running instance, AWS begins charging for it.
explanation.why: Always remember to release EIPs after terminating instances to avoid unexpected charges.

questions.question: A team is choosing between NAT Gateway and NAT Instance for a development environment with light traffic (< 1 GB/day). What is the primary advantage of using a NAT Instance in this scenario?

options.text: NAT Instance offers better performance
NAT Instance is easier to configure
NAT Instance can be cheaper for very low-traffic environments since you only pay for the EC2 instance
NAT Instance provides better security

explanation.correct: For very low-traffic dev/test scenarios, a NAT Instance running on a t2.micro or t3.micro can be cheaper than a NAT Gateway (which charges hourly + per GB processed).
explanation.why: NAT Gateway is preferred for production due to managed availability, auto-scaling, and zero maintenance. For low-traffic dev, NAT Instance can reduce costs.
